transcript:
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Windsor Johnston.
Hurricane NOLO is making its way toward Hawaii with heavy rain and dangerous surf threatening
the Big Island.
President Darren Montevo is filling sandbags after hearing how much rain could fall.
And I was like, "What?
We better do this, then.
That's a lot of rain."
Across the Pacific, Hurricane Polo is moving toward Mexico's Baja California Peninsula.
Forecasters warn it could bring dangerous surf and heavy rain to the region.
Along the East Coast, millions of people are bracing for a nor'easter that's expected
to bring strong winds and coastal flooding this weekend.
President Trump will travel to Tennessee today to watch a highly anticipated college football
matchup.
Jackie Sieber of member station WUOT reports the visit is stirring mixed reaction from
students.
Trump's presence comes as the University of Tennessee's campus is already teaming
with activity for ESPN's College Game Day show.
Student Cooper Dabs participated in festivities hosted by ESPN.
"It's just going to be a great environment.
I think we have a good shot at winning if the fans help out."
Student Amber Henderson looks forward to the game, but has reservations.
"I don't think that the game is about football anymore.
I think it's more so about politics."
Students are expected to see heightened security as they enter the stadium.
For NPR News, I'm Jackie Sieber in Knoxville.
Iran says it's presented the U.S. with a seven-day proposal to reopen the Strait of
Hormuz and end hostilities in the waterway.
NPR's Hadil al-Shaochi reports the Iranian foreign minister says Tehran would be ready
to execute the plan as soon as the Trump administration accepted.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Arafchi told reporters that Iran was ready to execute a
seven-day plan to begin talks about its nuclear program if the U.S. accepted.
The proposal is very close to a memorandum of understanding that the two countries agreed
upon in June.
That agreement established a framework for the U.S. to lift a naval blockade, ease sanctions
and free up Iranian assets in return for reopening the Strait of Hormuz and going back to talks
about Iran's nuclear program.
The U.S. has not responded publicly to the proposal.
In his speech to the U.N. General Assembly, President Trump said that Iran should accept
a deal or face "annihilation."
Hadil al-Shaochi, NPR News, Istanbul.
Tech giant OpenAI says its agents access public information on U.S. government websites, including
those of the Census Bureau and the Securities and Exchange Commission.
Researchers also say an agent tried and failed to break into an Education Department website.
OpenAI says it's found no evidence of stolen credentials or a data breach.
The company is reviewing the activity as it investigates cases where its AI systems acted
in unexpected ways.
This is NPR News.
American farmers closely watched Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to the White House this
week.
They've lost billions of dollars in sales to China as a result of President Trump's
tariffs.
South Dakota Public Broadcasting's Jackson Dirks reports from a farm outside of Sioux
Falls.
"And you put it into the combine."
Farmer Jeff Thompson is giving a tour of his soybean field.
These beans could be affected by conversations happening half a country away, and Thompson
is hoping for positive developments.
"You know, keep dialects open and level heads both ways."
When disputes have gone south, China stopped purchasing U.S. soybeans.
About 30 percent of South Dakota soybeans go to China, meaning producers here feel trade
disruptions caused by tariffs.
Another farmer, Kevin Scott, says it's not the producer's fault.
"It was government relations that were not great."
President Trump has won South Dakota by double-digit margins in the last three elections.
For NPR News, I'm Jackson Dirks in Sioux Falls, South Dakota.
Mortgage rates increased this week.
Freddie Mac says the average rate on a 30-year fixed mortgage reached just over 7 percent,
up from 6.9 percent last week.
That raises monthly payments for buyers and may keep some homeowners from selling if moving
would mean giving up a lower rate.
A bond market sell-off has helped push rates higher.
Investors are demanding higher returns on bonds amid inflation concerns, and mortgage
rates tend to rise with them.
I'm Windsor Johnston, NPR News, in Washington.
